steps.title: Building with blocks
paragraphs: Think of clauses as building blocks.
A simple sentence is one block. A compound sentence is two blocks side by side. A complex sentence is one block with a smaller block leaning on it.
Now put them all together: two big blocks side by side, and a small one leaning on one of them. That’s a compound-complex sentence.
“When the bell rang, the students cheered, and the teacher smiled.”

cards.title: The recipe
cards.body: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Compound (two independents) + complex (a dependent) = compound-complex.

cards.title: Find the parts
cards.text:
When the storm hit, the lights went out, and we lit candles.
Dependent: When the storm hit
Independent 1: the lights went out
Independent 2: we lit candles
cards.note: Comma after the opening dependent clause, and a comma before “and” where the second independent clause begins.

cards.title: Use them sparingly
cards.body: One or two compound-complex sentences can tie ideas together beautifully, often near the end of a paragraph. A whole paragraph of them is exhausting to read.

prompts: Take one of your compound-complex sentences apart. What are its clauses?
When might a compound-complex sentence be too much for the reader?
